must_fix: Replace the weekly OOS scoring window with a cadence matched to Qloo's actual refresh dates (the ~40-50 move weeks) or explicitly exclude the frozen newest ~8 weeks, because a constant regressor in the final OOS weeks makes the refit interval unidentified there.

Drop the observed-spread power criterion and state power against a pre-specified minimum meaningful effect (e.g., the smallest ΔR² the desk would treat as a real channel); report that power instead of, or alongside, the observed-spread figure.

Replace the intersection-union rule (every null at p ≤ 0.10) with a single pre-specified primary null and report the others as sensitivity checks, because requiring three correlated nulls to clear makes NO SIGNAL the near-certain outcome even under a true effect.
Print the active-week count (19-31) as an identification flag on every per-name page and exclude names below a pre-registered floor rather than publishing weakly identified betas alongside the rest.
method_objections: The claim that the analytic variance benchmark is 'the miscalibrated one' because it overshoots by 25% inside the rotation null does not follow: the same 25% gap can be generated by shared-calendar cross-name covariance, heteroskedasticity, or the rotation null's imposed dependence structure, so the inference is not identified.

The intersection-union grading rule (every null at p ≤ 0.10) would suppress a real effect: with three correlated nulls derived from the same returns, requiring all three to clear makes NO SIGNAL the near-certain outcome and is not a valid test of absence.

The OOS refit interval [−2.12, +0.64] is used to 'bound what the window can exclude,' but with 35 weekly OOS weeks and a regressor frozen in the newest ~8 weeks, the refit is weakly identified and the interval is too wide to exclude effects of any practical size.

The per-name cultural beta is identified from only 19-31 active weeks (median 29) out of 102, so the median |t| of 0.60 and the zero flags reflect weak identification rather than evidence of no effect; publishing them as a calibrated book overstates what is identified.
overstatements: Phrase: 'the wider interval bounds what the window can exclude' — Correction: it does not; with 35 OOS weeks and a frozen regressor in the final ~8 weeks, the interval is too wide to exclude effects of practical size and should be read as uninformative.

Phrase: 'the factor was looked for and not detectable at this window length' — Correction: the dispersion test has 0% power at the observed spread (sd 28.4), so non-detection is uninformative, not a demonstration of non-detectability.

Phrase: 'every null matches' — Correction: the three nulls are correlated transformations of the same data; 'every null matches' is not evidence of absence and the intersection-union rule guarantees NO SIGNAL even under a true effect.
verdict.dispersion_verdict: Yes — the rotation-null calibration is sound and the 'uninformative' reading is correct, because power at the observed spread is 0% and the statistic cannot distinguish the measured dispersion from noise.
verdict.power_criterion_verdict: No — power at the observed spread anchors the test on the estimate under test, which is circular; the right criterion is power at a pre-specified minimum meaningful effect, and by that standard the test is also uninformative (power ≈ 0% at any plausible effect).
verdict.best_next_model_construction: Re-estimate at Qloo's native refresh cadence: collapse to the ~40-50 weeks where the percentile actually moves (or monthly), use only those as effective observations, and re-run the same falsification battery rather than forcing weekly OLS on a piecewise-constant regressor.
verdict.headline_rewrite: Across 80 priced consumer names, Qloo taste beta adds no detectable weekly return beyond SPY (OOS ΔR² −0.05 pts; all nulls p > 0.77); the desk publishes the null, the code, and the cached responses.
verdict.judge_60s: Most likely to misread the published NO SIGNAL grade as evidence that Qloo taste data is useless, when the correct reading is that this particular weekly, piecewise-constant basket at this cadence and window had no detectable incremental power — a data/identification limitation, not a refutation of taste as a channel.

must_fix: Replace 'power at the observed spread' as the reading key with a pre-specified minimum detectable spread (MDE at 80% power) printed next to the dispersion table, and state on the read page that at this MDE the desk cannot distinguish NO SIGNAL from FAILS.

Make Qloo load-bearing visible in the product: add a per-sub-sector panel comparing the Qloo basket's return path against the no-Qloo peer basket (correlation, active-week overlap, dispersion), so judges see what the Qloo data contributes rather than inferring it from two nulls.
Support 'all four fields move at the same cadence' with week-level co-movement of change indicators across fields, not medians; medians of 39-50 changing weeks do not establish identical timing.

Print the effective-sample bound up front: ~29 shared active weeks out of 102, piecewise-constant levels, 8 frozen weeks — a reader should know before the results that this window was close to guaranteed non-detection.
method_objections: Power at the observed spread is endogenous: it anchors on an estimate that is itself near zero, so 0% power conflates 'the test is weak' with 'the effect is small.' The correct criterion is power at a pre-registered minimal effect size, or equivalently reporting the MDE the refit interval already implies (~2.1 pts). The observed-spread figure is defensible as a diagnostic but not as the sole key to 'informative.'

The benchmark reconciliation's conclusion (analytic mean-se² is the miscalibrated yardstick) holds, but the stated mechanism is incomplete: inside the rotation null the basket link is severed, yet cross-name residual covariance — shared calendar, common sector shocks, correlated omitted factors — independently pushes cross-sectional slope variance below the sum of marginal variances. The overshoot therefore does not isolate 'treats 80 slopes as independent' as the sole defect; the team should attribute it to both cross-name dependence channels, which actually strengthens the case against the analytic benchmark.

'A positive claim requires every null at p ≤ 0.10 (intersection-union)' is a mislabel: IUT applies to decomposing a composite hypothesis into components, not to testing the same hypothesis three ways. What the team has built is a conservative max-of-p rule; harmless here because every p is 0.78-0.93, but the framing should be corrected before a statistician on the panel flags it.

The dispersion test with 0% power at every planted spread up to sd 50 is not 'calibrated' — it is disclosed as uninformative, which is different. 'Now calibrated, and it reports itself as uninformative' is internally contradictory; the honest phrasing is that calibration of the reading was added, and the reading is that the statistic has no resolving power at this sample.
overstatements: 'all four weekly fields in that response move at the same slow cadence' — supported only by medians (39-50 of ~198 weeks); correct to 'no field shows materially more weekly movement than the others by median change frequency; week-level co-movement not verified.'

'The dispersion test — now calibrated' — a test with 0% power at the observed spread was not calibrated; correct to 'the dispersion test's reading is now keyed to a disclosed power figure and reports uninformative.'

'A block permutation respecting the cadence would confirm the p-values' (round 3 header as recapitulated) — p 0.830 vs 0.778 agrees with, and does not confirm, the week-by-week figure; 'agrees with' is the correct verb.
verdict.dispersion_verdict: Yes with one caveat — the independent-rotation null and the uninformative reading are right, but the reconciliation over-attributes the 25% overshoot to the independence assumption when cross-name residual covariance is an equally admissible mechanism, and the test's 0% power means 'uninformative' must not be read as evidence of homogeneity in either direction.
verdict.power_criterion_verdict: No — power anchored on the observed (near-zero) spread begs the question; key the reading on power at a pre-specified minimal spread or state the MDE, which the refit interval already bounds at roughly a 2.1-point effect.
verdict.best_next_model_construction: Aggregate to the cadence the data actually supports: test the taste factor at monthly or quarterly horizon (matching the ~4-7 week refresh and revision structure) with returns and basket steps aligned to the natural refresh grid, restoring effective sample where the weekly construction has almost none.
verdict.headline_rewrite: One pre-registered test across 80 consumer names finds Qloo taste-basket timing too sparse in this window to detect or rule out a cultural beta — so the desk ships the evidence trail, the power bounds, and the negative result, not the claim.
verdict.judge_60s: A skimming judge will most likely read 'NO SIGNAL' as 'Qloo data does not matter for equities' when the actual finding is that /v2/trending's refresh cadence cannot support a weekly-horizon test at all — a sampling-frequency limitation, not a verdict on the taste channel; the converse misread, that the peer-basket ablation proves Qloo adds value, is equally wrong since both baskets are nulls.

must_fix: Add a one-sentence legend to the dispersion table: 'Power at observed spread = 0% means this test cannot distinguish the heterogeneity it measured from noise; it does not mean the heterogeneity is real.'
Print the power-at-observed-spread figure in the same font size as the p-value, not as a footnote to the table.

Add a two-sentence explicit distinction between NO SIGNAL and FAILS in the grade legend: 'NO SIGNAL means the test lacked power to detect the effect size observed; FAILS means a negative effect was measured with a confidence interval clear of zero.'
method_objections: The observed-spread power criterion is circular in the weak sense that it anchors the power benchmark on the quantity being tested. A test that cannot detect the spread it measured is underpowered, but the criterion does not distinguish 'the effect is real but we cannot see it' from 'the effect is noise.' The correct criterion is power at a pre-specified minimum detectable effect (e.g., ΔR² ≥ 0.5 pts OOS), not at the observed spread. Here the criterion produces the right reading (uninformative) but for the wrong reason.

The benchmark reconciliation assumes the rotation null is the ground truth and the analytic figure is wrong. But the rotation null could itself be miscalibrated if the independent rotation of each name's basket does not reproduce the covariance structure of the real betas. The 25% overshoot is consistent with the independence assumption being wrong, but also with the rotation null being too narrow. The conclusion is plausible but not proven.

The intersection-union rule across three nulls (rotation, date-perm, block-perm) is conservative by construction and will suppress real effects. With 80 names and ~100 weeks, the test has low power against any but large effects. The rule is appropriate for a pre-registered falsification, but the team should state explicitly that a real cultural beta smaller than ~2 pts OOS ΔR² would fail to clear this grade even if genuine.

The pooled panel result (within-ΔR² +0.04 pts, p 0.928) is not integrated into the grade. The panel is a different estimator from the per-name OOS, and its p-value is reported but not used in the intersection-union. If the panel is the primary specification, its p should be in the rule; if the per-name OOS is primary, the panel should be labeled a sensitivity and not printed alongside the grade.
overstatements: In the desk copy: 'the factor was looked for and not detectable at this window length' — this implies the window is the only limitation. The correct statement is: 'the factor was looked for and not detectable at this window length with this sample size and this endpoint cadence; the test had 0% power against the heterogeneity it measured.'

In the brief: 'A test that would miss a genuine heterogeneity as large as the one it measured, even if that heterogeneity were entirely real, has not tested anything' — this overstates. The test has tested something (calibrated the null correctly); it has simply failed to confirm the alternative. The correction: 'A test with 0% power at the observed spread cannot distinguish the measured heterogeneity from noise, so the result is uninformative about whether cultural beta is real.'

In the brief: 'the grade is read off the refit interval; the page says the wider interval bounds what the window can exclude, which here is only effects larger than ~2.1 pts' — this framing implies the interval is a meaningful bound. The correction: 'the 90% refit interval for OOS ΔR² is [-2.12, +0.64]; effects larger than 2.12 pts in either direction are excluded, but effects of any smaller magnitude are not excluded, including zero.'
verdict.dispersion_verdict: Yes, the 'uninformative' reading is correct — a test with 0% power at the spread it measured cannot distinguish that spread from noise — but the criterion is circular and should be replaced with power at a pre-specified minimum detectable effect.
verdict.power_criterion_verdict: No, anchoring power on the observed spread begs the question: it asks whether the test can detect what it measured, not whether the measured effect is real. The right criterion is power at a principled minimum detectable effect (e.g., the smallest cultural beta that would matter for portfolio construction), not at the observed sd.
verdict.best_next_model_construction: Extend the window to the maximum Qloo coverage (2022-07) with a pre-registered split: the first 80% of weeks for estimation, last 20% for scoring, and report power at the minimum detectable ΔR² rather than at the observed spread.
verdict.headline_rewrite: Cultural beta was pre-registered as a falsifiable risk factor; 102 weeks of Qloo taste-basket data and 80 names produced no detectable signal in out-of-sample tests, and the dispersion test lacked power to confirm the heterogeneity it measured.
verdict.judge_60s: A judge skimming for 60 seconds will read 'NO SIGNAL' as 'nothing was found' and miss that the in-sample +0.67 pts is also reported prominently; they may conclude the desk is claiming a positive result when the grade explicitly says otherwise. The fix is to move the grade and the OOS interval to the top of the evidence page, before the in-sample table.
